title: jemalloc-threadwake-tiny-hz-tail-latency-sleuthing
content:
Context:
This is a focused investigation notes doc for a recurring category of tail-latency spikes we see on CPU-heavy small requests (~10-200 tokens). Symptoms appear in hosted API p50/p95 gap widening during steady traffic with many concurrent tiny requests (chat ping, single-short prompts). Previous tokenization and JSON-parse probes covered earlier layers; this thread explores allocator + thread wake/sleep interactions, Python scheduler noise, and how tiny allocations amplify wakeups and contention when using our default memory allocator.

Why this feels different:
- Spikes correlate with request churn (many short-lived requests) rather than long decode tails.
- Flamegraphs show lots of time in malloc/free hot paths and futex wakeups around worker handoffs.
- Enabling jemalloc tuning knobs reduced p95 in a small self-hosted cluster, but not repeatable across instance types.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Small-allocation churn + jemalloc arenas contends across many threads causing futex waits on arena metadata -> increases tail.
2) Worker threadpark/unpark and Python thread scheduling (GIL handoff) add jitter; combined with allocator futexing yields long tails.
3) Syscall scheduler/coalescing and CPU frequency governors amplify the above under power-saving modes.
4) Tokenization/parse is still contributing but is not the dominant time-sink for the observed spikes.

Quick observations from traces (summary):
- perf script flamegraphs show repeated stacks: worker-handoff -> pthread_cond_wait/futex -> jemalloc:arena_run -> mallocx -> small-object free
- Samples bucketed around request boundaries (hand-off wakeups ~1.5-3ms per occurrence on affected hosts)
- Hosts with libstdc++/jemalloc mismatches show higher variance

What we ran (experiments):
1) Repro harness: synthetic driver that issues 500 RPS of 20-token requests with 64 concurrent client threads. Server binary built with profiling enabled (perf, tcmalloc-jemalloc variant).
Commands used:
- perf record -F 99 -g --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> -- sleep 120
- ./flamegraph.pl perf.fold > perf-journal.svg

2) Allocator swap: binary builds with:
- system malloc (glibc)
- jemalloc default
- jemalloc with MALLOC_CONF="narenas:4,lg_dirty_mult:0.5,background_thread:false"
Measured p50/p95/p99 across runs.

3) Threadpark microbench: instrumented worker yield/park/unpark to add counters and measure latency between unpark and first useful work.
- Added high-res monotonic timestamps at park/unpark and on first token emitted.

4) CPU governor experiments: ondemand vs performance mode.

Results (numbers are representative averages):
- baseline (jemalloc default): p95 = 42ms, p99 = 123ms
- jemalloc narenas:4 tuned: p95 = 28ms, p99 = 67ms
- glibc malloc: p95 = 31ms, p99 = 80ms
- jemalloc tuned + performance governor: p95 = 20ms, p99 = 45ms
- threadpark-instrumentation showed median unpark->work 0.9ms, 95th 7.8ms; correlated high samples with jemalloc arena futex contention windows

Interpretation/what likely happened:
- Small-request patterns cause many threads to allocate/free small buffers frequently. Default jemalloc creates many arenas (one per core heuristically) and can cause cross-thread contention when per-thread allocation affinity mismatches.
- When a worker frees memory that maps to another arena or when arena metadata needs update, threads may block on futexes deep in allocator code. Those futex waits overlap with threadpark/unpark events, compounding tail latency.
- CPU governor (power saving) increased wake latency and amplified p99 differences.

Artifacts from runs (notes):
- perf flame excerpts attached in linked_artifacts (see GITHUB-PR-8812 for perf SVGs)
- Heap profile snapshots show a lot of short-lived 64B-512B objects (token buffers, small JSON objects)

Mitigations tried and outcomes:
1) jemalloc narenas reduction: reduces metadata contention for small objects on our workload. Helpful on x86 and AWS C6i instances. Risk: internal fragmentation increase on scale-up.
2) Explicit per-thread allocator arenas (TLS) - patching runtime allocator to bind worker threads to arenas gave best p95 wins but required careful integration with Python worker threads. Complexity high.
3) Switching to glibc malloc: sometimes reduced p99 but increased median CPU usage and memory highwater; inconsistent.
4) Introduced a tiny allocation pool (lock-free freelist) for 64B/128B buffers in C++ side used by tokenizer and request preparse. This removed many allocations from the general allocator and improved stability.
5) Aggressive CPU governor to performance: reduces wake latency but increases power/cost. Workload dependent.

Short-term recommendations (fast experiments):
- Add a small fixed-size freelist for token + header buffers on hot path (C++): low-risk, low-effort, measurable.
- Set MALLOC_CONF defaults in our runtime container images to narenas:4 and lg_dirty_mult:0.25 as an experiment in the dedicated fleet (A/B flag via runtime config). Track p50/p95/p99 and memory RSS.
- Add threadpark instrumentation as a lightweight debug mode to production builds (toggle via env) so we can correlate unpark jitter with allocation hotspots without full perf.

Longer-term ideas (workstreams):
- Per-worker allocator domain: design a safe binding for Python worker threads (consider subinterpreters or dedicated worker processes) to allow arena affinity without breaking Python C-extensions.
- Move more preproc/tokenization to a small pool of persistent threads (pinned) that amortize allocations instead of spawning free-for-all on request threads.
- Evaluate jemalloc background_thread:true (experimentally) to offload some maintenance, but watch for interference with our threadpool latency.
- Formal microbench suite for small-object allocation patterns (parametric over concurrency and request size) and continuous benchmark reporting in Perf Board.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why some instance types still show higher p99 after the same jemalloc tuning? (Possible kernel, NUMA, IRQ affinity differences.)
- Interaction with Python GIL handoffs and C-extension allocations: how to measure without impacting latency?
- Memory fragmentation trade-offs long-run when reducing arenas - what is real-world RSS growth on heavy sustained traffic?

Next actions (owners & timeline):
- Marco: implement small freelist for 64/128B buffers in tokenizer module (PR in 1 week)
- Lena: bake MALLOC_CONF into canary container images and run 3-day soak on dedicated cluster (start this week)
- Priya: add threadpark instrumentation and a lightweight dashboard correlating unpark latency with alloc/free hotspots (PR + dashboard in 2 weeks)
- Sanjay (me): drive system-level perf runs and assemble a benchmark that can be re-run in CI; write a doc summarizing safe production knobs once experiments stabilize (2–3 weeks)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc intentionally focuses on allocator + wake interactions; there are multiple other docs about parsing/tokenization micro-optimizations. If you are combining findings, please cross-link rather than duplicate.
- Attached traces and perf SVGs are in the PR (GITHUB-PR-8812). I left raw perf.data in the temp trace bucket for anyone who wants to replay.

Appendix: quick commands (repro tips)
- Run repro load:
  ./tests/repro_driver --rps 500 --concurrency 64 --size 20 --duration 120
- Collect perf:
  sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pidof server) -- sleep 120
  sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.fold
  ./flamegraph.pl perf.fold > perf.svg
- jemalloc override for local run:
  export MALLOC_CONF="narenas:4,lg_dirty_mult:0.25,background_thread:false"
  ./server-binary --config=local-debug.yaml

End of notes.
